comparison: Both evaluate the core CITE-seq methodology (C27-C32). OpenEval finds the approach well-documented and reproducible. Peer reviewers affirm the methodology as 'carefully conducted' with 'very clearly presented' results, but note the limited sample size (9 CML patients, 2 healthy donors) as a weakness requiring additional samples to strengthen findings.

Both evaluate inter-patient heterogeneity findings (C4, C37-C38). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers fully support this finding, with peer reviewers explicitly stating 'substantial cellular heterogeneity was observed at diagnosis, suggesting that this is a hallmark of CML' and highlighting it as a fundamental insight.

Both evaluate treatment outcome associations with primitive cell frequencies (C5, C39-C41). OpenEval notes support but raises concerns about limited statistical details and small sample sizes (n=4 optimal, n=2 failures). Peer reviewers strongly support the finding (C42 also included in peer evaluation), emphasizing validation through independent dataset deconvolution and describing the evidence as 'convincing.'

Both address deconvolution validation (C42-C43). OpenEval supports the external validation approach though notes limited p-value details. Peer reviewers support these observations (C43, C44) as part of the study rationale, implicitly accepting them within the robust methodology.

Both evaluate differential cluster abundance and gene expression patterns (C33-C36). OpenEval finds the pan-CML signature approach methodologically sound. Peer reviewers do not explicitly critique these findings and implicitly accept them as part of the 'robust methodology' providing 'compelling evidence.'

Both evaluate BCR::ABL1+ and BCR::ABL1- population separation (C46-C48 overlap, plus C6-C8 in peer review). OpenEval supports the stem cell-enriched fraction analysis. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this as a 'major new contribution,' emphasizing the use of gene expression profiles to distinguish populations and show association with TKI response.

Both evaluate differential expression signatures (C50-C53). OpenEval supports the identification of known CML markers in BCR::ABL1+ signature and HSC-related genes in BCR::ABL1- signature. Peer reviewers do not challenge these findings and describe the methodology as 'carefully conducted' with 'very clearly presented' results.

Both evaluate ADT analysis and CD26/CD35 marker identification (C56-C57, C59 overlap). OpenEval highlights CD35 as a novel HSC marker with strong quantitative support. Peer reviewers explicitly support this as a 'key contribution,' noting it 'will allow for more detailed interrogation of these cell populations at a molecular level.'

Both evaluate the CD26/CD35 sorting approach (C62-C64 overlap, plus C7-C8 in OpenEval). OpenEval emphasizes high capture efficiency and purity as a novel practical advance. Peer reviewers affirm this finding overlaps with their R4 evaluation, noting the marker combination can 'prospectively isolate the two populations.'

OpenEval R9 also addresses validation aspects (C65-C66 overlap with peer R5). OpenEval supports the ADT gating analysis documentation. Peer reviewers affirm 'CD26 and CD35 expression can consistently identify BCR-ABL+ versus BCR-ABL- cells' with qPCR validation confirming the marker combination's capacity.

Both evaluate qPCR validation (C67-C69, with C67 overlap). OpenEval emphasizes orthogonal validation at diagnosis and post-treatment with GAS2 expression providing additional molecular validation. Peer reviewers affirm this as part of confirming 'key observations in additional samples.'

Both evaluate qPCR validation findings (C68-C69 overlap). OpenEval supports the validation strengthening confidence in the marker combination. Peer reviewers affirm the validation without challenge, noting it confirms the capacity to separate populations.

Both evaluate longitudinal treatment outcome associations (C9-C10, C73-C76, C80). OpenEval supports the clinical relevance but notes limited sample sizes (n=6 optimal, n=5 failures) and calls for more comprehensive statistical details. Peer reviewers explicitly support the finding, emphasizing differences in CD26-CD35+ primitive stem cell proportions between responders and failures at both diagnosis and 3 months post-treatment.

Both evaluate cell cycle/quiescence findings (C71-C72). OpenEval supports these findings as important for understanding TKI resistance mechanisms. Peer reviewers do not challenge these observations and implicitly accept them as part of the 'carefully conducted' methodology.

OpenEval evaluates quantitative validation of known CML markers (C49) with clear fold-change ranges supporting LSC identification. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this specific claim.

Both address limitations of existing markers (C44). OpenEval supports this finding as motivating the CD26/CD35 approach. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this observation (C44 in their R12) as part of the study rationale within the robust methodology.

Both address variable BCR::ABL1+/- ratios across patients (C6). OpenEval supports this finding demonstrating inter-patient heterogeneity. Peer reviewers include C6 in their evaluation of the major contribution regarding population separation and its association with TKI response.

OpenEval evaluates additional surface marker patterns and hierarchical relationships (C91-C94, C96-C97), noting the CD26-CD35- interpretation as MPPs is reasonable but somewhat inferential. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

OpenEval evaluates established CML background knowledge (C1-C3, C11-C20) as appropriately cited context, not novel findings. No corresponding peer review evaluation found as reviewers focus on novel contributions rather than background claims.

OpenEval evaluates extensive prior work citations (C21-C26, C60-C61, C70, C77-C95) as appropriate foundation for the study. No corresponding peer review evaluation found as reviewers focus on novel findings rather than literature citations.
